title: The map in your pocket
text: The map in your pocket knows where you are to within a few metres, and it {{1}} the strange arithmetic of Einstein to do it. Two dozen satellites orbit 20,000 kilometres overhead, each {{2}} its position and the exact time, measured by atomic clocks, at which the signal left. Your phone receives messages from several satellites and {{3}} its distance from each by how late the signals arrive — a timing job so delicate that a billionth of a second {{4}} to a thirty-centimetre error. And here is where Einstein {{5}}: time runs measurably faster on the satellites than on the ground, because they sit further from Earth's gravity, while their speed slows their clocks by a smaller {{6}}. The two effects do not cancel; left uncorrected, they would accumulate to some ten kilometres of error per day, {{7}} the whole system useless within minutes. The satellites' clocks are therefore deliberately offset before launch. Relativity, a theory often {{8}} as remote from daily life, is thus quietly consulted every time you find a restaurant — the most practical physics most people will ever use.

gaps.explanation: 'it borrows the arithmetic of Einstein' — makes use of it; burrow = dig a tunnel.
'each broadcasting its position and time' — transmitting them continuously; brace = steady oneself.
'deduces its distance from each' — reasons it out from the evidence; reduce, shrink and shorten would make it smaller.
'a billionth of a second amounts to a thirty-centimetre error' — 'amount to' = be equivalent to; mount = climb or increase (mount up).
'here is where Einstein enters' — comes into the account; embark takes 'on', elbow = push with the arm.

gaps.hint: an amount by which something differs
gaps.explanation: 'slows their clocks by a smaller margin' — by a smaller difference; morsel = a small bite of food.
'rendering the whole system useless' — making it so; render + object + adjective is the fixed pattern.
'a theory often dismissed as remote' — written off as irrelevant; disperse = scatter, despair takes 'of'.
